pages.text: King Arthur is the great legend of Britain: a once and future king who will return when Britain needs him most, sleeping somewhere under a hill with his knights around him. He may have been a real war leader in the fifth or sixth century, fighting the Germanic invaders who were moving into what is now England after the withdrawal of the Roman legions. Or he may be entirely invented. The stories don't care. They have been growing for fifteen hundred years regardless.

image.note: Illustration: Excalibur embedded in a stone on a hilltop, early morning mist, no one yet arrived to pull it out

pages.text: The legend as most people know it was largely assembled in the fifteenth century by the English knight Thomas Malory, who wrote Le Morte d'Arthur while in prison and completed it in 1469. Malory drew on French romances, Welsh legends, and English traditions to create the most complete version of the story: the Round Table, the quest for the Holy Grail, Lancelot, Guinevere, Merlin, and the fall of Camelot.

The legend endures because it contains several things simultaneously: a story about the possibility of just government, a story about the impossibility of perfection, a love story, and a tragedy. It is about what people build when they try their hardest, and what happens when human weakness is too strong for even the best intentions.

When the High King of Britain died without an heir, chaos threatened. Merlin, the great wizard, set a sword in a stone in a churchyard, with an inscription: whoever pulls this sword from the stone is the rightful King of Britain. The greatest knights in the land tried. None could move it.

image.note: Illustration: a young boy pulling a sword from a stone, looking as surprised as everyone else

pages.text: Arthur was a squire, the younger son of a minor nobleman, sent to a tournament to fetch his older brother's sword. He forgot it and, looking for something quickly, found the sword in the stone in the churchyard. He pulled it out without difficulty. He put it back and pulled it out again, just to be sure. He took it to his brother, who asked where he had got it.

The greatest knights tried again, in front of witnesses, to pull the sword from the stone. None could. Arthur drew it again, easily. He was fifteen years old. He did not look like a king. He did not feel like a king. He was a king.

No figure in the Arthur legends is stranger or more important than Merlin. Part prophet, part magician, part wise counsellor, Merlin arranges Arthur's very birth, hides him away as a child, and sets the sword in the stone that will reveal the true king. Throughout Arthur's rise, Merlin stands at his shoulder, seeing further than other men, warning of dangers still to come. He is the wisdom behind the throne, and while he guides it, Camelot flourishes.

But Merlin's own tale ends in a very human way. For all his power to see the future, he falls in love, and the enchantress he loves coaxes his secrets from him and uses his own magic to imprison him forever, in some tellings beneath a great stone, in others inside an oak. The wisest man in the world is undone by his own heart. Even in a story full of magic, the Arthur legends keep returning to this truth: that the strongest people are brought down not from outside, but from within.

Arthur wanted his knights to sit at a table with no head, so that no one knight was higher than another. Merlin provided the Round Table, which could seat 150 knights. Arthur built Camelot, the finest court in the world. Knights came from across Europe to join it. The Round Table was not a piece of furniture. It was an idea: that power could be shared, that the strongest should serve the weakest, that justice was more important than rank.

image.note: Illustration: the Round Table from above, knights seated all around, no seat elevated above another

pages.text: The greatest of the knights were Lancelot, the finest fighter alive; Gawain, honourable and loyal; Percival, pure of heart; Galahad, who alone was destined to achieve the Grail; and Tristan, whose love story rivalled Arthur's own in its sadness. Each knight had a character. The Round Table was not simply a collection of excellent fighters. It was a community of people trying to live up to an ideal.
Inevitably, the ideal was too high. No community of human beings sustains perfection forever. The cracks began, as they often do, with the people who loved each other.

Lancelot, the greatest knight, loved Guinevere, Arthur's queen. Guinevere loved Lancelot. Arthur knew, and did not want to know, because Lancelot was the best of his knights and Guinevere was the person he loved most in the world. For years, the unspoken truth held.

image.note: Illustration: Arthur at a window of Camelot, alone, looking out over fields at dusk

pages.text: Mordred, Arthur's illegitimate son and his enemy, forced the truth into the open. Guinevere was condemned. Lancelot rescued her, killing several knights in the process, including Gawain's brothers. The fellowship of the Round Table broke apart along the lines of the old loyalties. Arthur pursued Lancelot to France. While he was away, Mordred seized the kingdom.

Arthur returned. At the Battle of Camlann, nearly everyone died. Mordred and Arthur killed each other. The surviving knights took Arthur to the island of Avalon to heal from his wounds. He did not return. He has not returned yet.

At the centre of the later tales lies the quest for the Holy Grail, the sacred cup, which appears in a vision at Camelot and sends every knight riding out to find it. The Grail quest is the noblest adventure of the Round Table and also its undoing, for it scatters the fellowship across the world, and only the purest knights come close to the prize. Many never return. The very ideal that inspires the knights is the thing that empties Arthur's hall.

Here is the deep sadness woven through all the Arthur stories. Camelot is the dream of a better world, where the strong serve the weak and might is used for right. But it is built by flawed human beings, and their flaws, pride, jealousy, forbidden love, bring it down from the inside. The dream does not fail because it is wrong. It fails because the people who hold it are only people. That, more than any battle, is what has kept the legend alive for fifteen hundred years.

The Arthurian legend has been retold in every century since it was assembled, in every medium available in that century: manuscripts, plays, novels, operas, films, television series, and countless others. It has been told from Arthur's point of view, from Guinevere's, from Merlin's, from Lancelot's, and from Mordred's.

image.note: Illustration: a montage of different artistic depictions of Arthur across centuries

pages.text: It endures because it is about something that every person and every society faces: the attempt to build something good, the corruption that comes from inside, the destruction that follows, and the stubborn hope that something remains, sleeping under a hill, available to be called on when it is genuinely needed.
Once and future king. It is the best description of what we do with our ideals: we lose them. We wait. And eventually, when things are bad enough, we call them back.
